1: This article names the country and fixes its shape. India, that is Bharat, is a Union of States. The States and the Union territories are listed in the First Schedule. The territory of India also takes in any other territories the country may later acquire. A Union of States means one country built out of states under one Constitution.
2: This article gives Parliament the power to admit or establish new States in the Union. Admission or establishment happens by law, on terms and conditions Parliament thinks fit. The article looks short, but it is the door through which new states have entered after 1950.
3: This article lets Parliament change the map of the States by law. It can form a new State by separating or uniting territory. It can increase or diminish the area of any State, alter its boundaries, or change its name. Such a Bill needs the President's recommendation. The concerned State may state its views, but its consent is not required.
4: This article handles what follows a boundary change. A law under article 2 or 3 can also amend the First and Fourth Schedules as needed. It may carry supplemental and consequential provisions, such as changes in representation. Such a law is not counted as an amendment of the Constitution under article 368.
5: This article settled who became a citizen when the Constitution began. A person with domicile in India became a citizen if born in India, or if either parent was born there, or after residing in India for five years before the commencement. It applied once, at the start, on 26 January 1950.
6: This article dealt with people who moved to India from Pakistan around Partition. Such a person was counted a citizen if a parent or grandparent was born in India as the law then defined it. Those who came after 19 July 1948 also needed registration after residence. The article settled citizenship for one migration at one moment in history.
7: This article covered movement the other way. A person who migrated from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 was not to be a citizen of India. There was one exception. A person who returned under a permit for resettlement could become a citizen after registration. The article kept citizenship from surviving a permanent move away.
8: This article covered people of Indian origin living abroad. It applied where the person, or a parent or grandparent, was born in India as then defined. The person also had to be living outside India. Such a person could become a citizen by registration. The registration was done by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
9: This article is short and firm. A person who voluntarily takes the citizenship of a foreign state cannot be a citizen of India under articles 5, 6, or 8. Citizenship at the commencement could not sit alongside another citizenship of the person's own free choice.
10: This article keeps citizenship going. Anyone who is a citizen under this Part continues to be one, subject to any law Parliament makes. Parliament may later set how citizenship continues or ends. The article bridged the opening rules of the Constitution and the citizenship laws that followed.
11: This article keeps Parliament's power open. Nothing in articles 5 to 10 limits Parliament's right to make laws on citizenship. Parliament may regulate how citizenship is acquired and lost, and all other matters relating to it. This power produced the Citizenship Act, 1955, which governs the subject today.
12: This article defines who counts as the State for this Part. The definition covers the Government and Parliament of India, state governments and legislatures, and local or other bodies under government control or within India. The rights in this Part bind all of these bodies.
13: This article makes fundamental rights stronger than ordinary law. Any law, old or new, that conflicts with these rights stops working to that extent. The word law covers ordinances, rules, orders, and customs. Governments cannot bypass rights by choosing a different legal form.
14: This article says every person is equal before the law and gets equal protection of the laws. The State cannot treat one person better or worse than another in like cases. Courts use it to test arbitrary state action, because unequal treatment without a fair reason usually fails here.
15: This article bans discrimination by the State against citizens only on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. No citizen can be barred from shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks, or public places on those grounds. The State may still make special provisions for women, children, and disadvantaged classes, and for seats in education and jobs.
16: This article promises an equal chance for all citizens to get public jobs. No citizen can be kept out of a government job only for reasons of religion, race, caste, sex, birth, family line, or residence. Parliament or a state legislature may set residence rules for some posts. The State may also reserve posts for backward classes.
17: This article abolishes untouchability. Its practice in any form is forbidden. So is enforcing any disability that arises from it. Parliament backed this with a criminal law against untouchability. No custom, and no payment, can justify treating any person as untouchable.
18: This article stops the State from giving or recognising titles of nobility, and no citizen may accept one from a foreign state. Awards for military or academic distinction are allowed. They cannot be used as titles attached to names. The aim is to keep citizens equal, without ranks the government can hand out.
19: This article gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression; assembly without arms; forming associations; movement; residence; and any profession or trade. Each freedom can face reasonable limits. The State may set limits for stated public reasons, such as security, public order, or the rights of others. Only citizens hold these freedoms.
20: This article protects people in criminal cases in three ways. A person cannot be punished under a law that was not in force when the act was done. A person cannot be tried and punished twice for the same offence. And a person cannot be forced to testify against himself. These protections apply to everyone, citizen or not.
21: This article says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except by a fair legal procedure. Courts have read it broadly. The right to life means a life with dignity, and it covers things like a clean environment, health, shelter, and privacy. It is the most used fundamental right in Indian courts.
22: This article protects people who are arrested. An arrested person must be told the reason. The person may consult a lawyer of choice. The person must be produced before a magistrate within twenty four hours. Preventive detention is allowed, but only under a fair procedure with advisory boards and time limits set by law.
23: This article bans traffic in human beings and forced labour in any form. No one can be made to work without pay, and bonded labour is illegal. The State may require compulsory service for a public purpose, such as during an emergency. It must not impose that service by religion, caste, or class.
24: This article bans employing children below fourteen in factories, mines, or other risky work. It protects children from labour that harms health and safety. It works with the right to education in Article 21A, so children study instead of doing dangerous work.
25: This article guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise, and spread religion, for all persons. The State may regulate religious activity for public order, morality, and health. It may also open Hindu religious institutions to all classes. Wearing and carrying kirpans counts as part of the Sikh religion.
26: This article lets every religious group manage its own affairs. A group may set up institutions, own property, and run them by its own faith. This holds subject to public order, morality, and health. The State may still pass laws for social reform, or for opening institutions to all classes.
27: This article stops the State from forcing any person to pay taxes whose money is used to promote one religion. Public money collected from all cannot be spent on the institutions of a single faith. This keeps the state out of religious promotion.
28: This article keeps religious teaching out of institutions maintained fully by government funds. Institutions that receive aid may give religious teaching, but only with consent. No student can be made to attend religious teaching or worship without the consent of a guardian.
29: This article protects the culture and language of any section of citizens, including minorities. Any citizen has the right to conserve a distinct language, script, or culture. No citizen can be denied entry to a State run institution only for reasons of religion, race, caste, or language.
30: This article gives religious and language minorities the right to start and run their own schools and colleges. The State cannot be unfair to such institutions when giving aid. Laws that control them must respect the minority's choice of what is taught and who teaches.
31: This article was omitted by the Constitution Forty fourth Amendment Act in 1978. It earlier made the right to property a fundamental right. Property is now only an ordinary legal right under Article 300A. The State may take property for public use with a valid law and a fair process.
32: This article is the right to enforce every other right in this Part. A person whose rights are broken may go straight to the Supreme Court. The Court can pass directions and writs such as habeas corpus and certiorari. This remedy is itself a fundamental right. It cannot be suspended except as the Constitution allows during an emergency.
33: This article lets Parliament limit or end the fundamental rights of members of the armed forces, police, and intelligence services. The limits exist so that they keep discipline and do their duties properly. This is why service rules can curb speech and association rights for those in the forces.
34: This article protects persons acting under martial law from suits for acts done in that role. It also lets Parliament shield officers and servants of the Union for acts done to keep or restore order in areas where martial law holds.
35: This article gives Parliament alone the power to make laws for enforcing the rights in this Part. That includes the power to fix punishment for acts the Constitution declares to be crimes. State legislatures cannot make such laws. This keeps the sanctions for rights uniform across the country.
36: This article defines one word for this Part. The State has the same meaning here as in Part III. It covers the Government and Parliament of India, state governments and legislatures, and local or other authorities under government control. The directive principles therefore guide every arm of the State.
37: This article sets the legal force of the directive principles. Courts cannot enforce them. Yet the principles are fundamental in the governance of the country, and the State must apply them in making laws. They guide; they do not bind like fundamental rights. This balance between ideal and law runs through Part IV.
38: This article asks the State to build a just social order. Justice, social, economic, and political, must inform all the institutions of national life. The State must secure and protect such an order. The State must also strive to reduce inequalities in income. And it must work to remove inequalities in status, facilities, and opportunities. These duties run among individuals and among groups in different areas or lines of work.
39: This article lists goals for State policy. Citizens, men and women equally, should have an adequate means of livelihood. The ownership of material resources should serve the common good. Wealth and means of production should not concentrate in few hands to the common harm. Men and women should get equal pay for equal work. Children should be protected from exploitation, and no one should be forced by need into work unsuited to their age or strength.
40: This article asks the State to organise village panchayats. These bodies should have such powers and authority as they need to work as units of self-government. The aim is democracy at the village level. The 73rd Amendment later gave panchayats constitutional status, regular elections, and a list of local subjects.
41: This article sets social goals for the State to pursue within its economic capacity. The State should make effective provision for the right to work, to education, and to public help in unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement. It also covers other cases of undeserved want. The promise is real, but it is shaped by what the economy can carry.
42: This article asks the State to secure just and humane conditions of work. It also directs the State to provide maternity relief. Rules on working hours, safety, and maternity benefit in Indian law draw on this principle. The article keeps the dignity of the worker in view.
43: This article asks the State to secure workers a living wage. Workers in farming, industry, or any other line should get work, a living wage, and conditions that allow a decent standard of life. They should also enjoy leisure and social and cultural opportunities. The State should in particular promote cottage industries, on an individual or cooperative basis.
44: This article asks the State to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens across India. A civil code covers matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption. At present these matters run on different personal laws for different communities. One common code would place every citizen under the same civil rules. The article says the State shall endeavour, so it stands as a goal, not a settled law.
45: This article now covers the earliest years of childhood. The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years. The original text promised free education up to the age of fourteen. The 86th Amendment moved that promise into Article 21A as a right, and gave this article its present form.
46: This article asks the State to promote, with special care, the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people. It names the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in particular. The State must protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation. Support in education and jobs for these groups draws on this principle.
47: This article makes nutrition, living standards, and public health primary duties of the State. The State must raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people. It must improve public health. The State should also endeavour to stop the consumption of intoxicating drinks and of drugs that injure health, except for medicinal purposes.
48: This article asks the State to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines. The State should take steps to preserve and improve the breeds. It should prohibit the slaughter of cows and calves and of other milch and draught cattle. The article joins farm modernisation with the protection of cattle.
49: This article makes the protection of national monuments an obligation of the State. It covers monuments, places, and objects of artistic or historic interest. They must be declared by law to be of national importance. The State must protect each one. It must save them from damage, disfigurement, destruction, removal, disposal, or export.
50: This article asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services. The aim is that officers who run the administration should not also decide cases. Separation protects fairness in trials. The criminal procedure reforms of 1973 carried this principle into practice.
51: This article sets out the country's aims abroad. The State shall promote international peace and security. It shall maintain just and honourable relations between nations. It shall foster respect for international law and treaty obligations. And it shall encourage the settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
52: This article creates the office of the President of India. It runs to a single line. The President is the head of the Union. The articles that follow set out how the President is elected, what the office may do, and how a President can leave office.
53: This article vests the executive power of the Union in the President. It is exercised directly or through officers subordinate to the President, in accordance with the Constitution. The supreme command of the defence forces also rests with the President, and law regulates its use. The article does not shift functions that existing law gives to states or other authorities. Parliament may still confer functions on other authorities.
54: This article sets up the election of the President. The President is elected by an electoral college. It consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States. For this purpose, State includes the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union territory of Puducherry. Nominated members do not vote.
55: This article sets the manner of the presidential election. There shall be uniformity in the scale of representation of the different States, as far as practicable. The value of each member's vote is worked out by formula. This keeps parity between the States as a whole and the Union. The election follows proportional representation by single transferable vote. Voting is by secret ballot.
56: This article fixes the President's term at five years from the date of entering office. The President may resign by writing under hand to the Vice-President. The President may also be removed for violation of the Constitution, through impeachment under article 61. A resignation is communicated by the Vice-President to the Speaker of the House of the People.
57: This article allows re-election. A person who holds, or has held, office as President is eligible for election to that office again. This holds subject to the other provisions of the Constitution. Several Presidents have served more than one term under this rule.
58: This article sets the qualifications for President. A candidate must be a citizen of India. The candidate must have completed thirty five years of age. And the candidate must be qualified for election to the House of the People. A person holding an office of profit under the Government of India, a State, or a controlled authority is not eligible. The President, Vice-President, Governors, and Ministers do not count as holding offices of profit here.
59: This article sets the conditions of the President's office. The President cannot be a member of Parliament or a state legislature. Any such seat falls vacant on election as President. The President cannot hold any other office of profit. The President may use the official residences without rent and draws emoluments set by Parliament. Those emoluments cannot be reduced during the term.
60: This article prescribes the oath for the President. Every President, and every person acting in that office, must make and subscribe an oath or affirmation before entering upon the office. It is made in the presence of the Chief Justice of India. In his absence, the senior-most available Judge of the Supreme Court administers it. The oath binds the President to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution.
61: This article sets the impeachment procedure for the President. The charge is for violation of the Constitution. Either House of Parliament may prefer it. The proposal needs fourteen days' notice in writing signed by at least one fourth of the members of that House. It must pass by a majority of two thirds of the total membership. The other House then investigates the charge. The President may appear and be represented. If that House sustains the charge by the same majority, the President stands removed from office.
62: This article covers the timing of presidential elections. An election for an expiring term must be completed before the term ends. If a vacancy arises by death, resignation, or removal, the election is held as soon as possible. It must happen within six months of the vacancy. A person elected to fill the vacancy is entitled to the full term of five years.
63: This article creates the office of the Vice-President of India. Like article 52, it runs to a single line. The Vice-President is the second highest office of the Union. Article 64 makes the Vice-President the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States.
64: This article makes the Vice-President the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States. The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha. The Vice-President cannot hold any other office of profit. While acting as President, the Vice-President does not perform the duties of Chairman. The same applies while discharging the President’s functions under article 65.
65: This article covers gaps in the presidency. The office may fall vacant by death, resignation, or removal. The Vice-President then acts as President until a new President is elected. The President may also be unable to act owing to absence, illness, or any other cause. The Vice-President then discharges the functions until the President resumes duty. While so acting, the Vice-President has all the powers and immunities of the President.
66: This article covers the election of the Vice-President. The electoral college consists of members of both Houses of Parliament. The election follows proportional representation by single transferable vote, by secret ballot. The Vice-President cannot be a member of Parliament or a state legislature. A candidate must be a citizen of India, at least thirty five years old, and qualified for election to the Council of States. A person holding an office of profit is not eligible.
67: This article fixes the Vice-President's term at five years. The Vice-President may resign by writing to the President. The Vice-President may also be removed by a resolution of the Council of States. The resolution must be agreed to by the House of the People. Notice of at least fourteen days is required, and the resolution must carry a majority of all the then members of the Council.
68: This article covers the timing of Vice-Presidential elections. An election for an expiring term must be completed before the term ends. If a vacancy arises by death, resignation, or removal, the election is held as soon as possible after it occurs. The person elected serves the full term, subject to article 67.
69: This article prescribes the oath for the Vice-President. The oath or affirmation is made before entering office. It is subscribed before the President, or a person appointed by the President for the purpose. The Vice-President swears true faith and allegiance to the Constitution.
70: This article is a safety valve. Parliament may make provision for the discharge of the President's functions in any contingency not covered by this Chapter. It fills gaps the framers could not list. A sudden situation with no President and no Vice-President in place would be handled under a law made here.
71: This article deals with election disputes for the President and the Vice-President. All doubts and disputes from such elections are decided by the Supreme Court, and its decision is final. If an election is declared void, acts done by that person in office stay valid until the date of the decision. Parliament may regulate the related matters by law. A vacancy in the electoral college does not invalidate an election.
72: This article gives the President the power of mercy. The President may grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment. The President may also suspend, remit, or commute a sentence. This covers court martial cases, offences against laws on the Union List, and death sentences. The Governor's power over a death sentence is not affected. This power is the last door of relief in the justice system.
73: This article defines the reach of the Union’s executive power. It extends to matters on which Parliament can make laws. It also covers rights, authority, and jurisdiction from any treaty or agreement. These are exercised by the Government of India. Until Parliament provides otherwise, states may keep exercising functions in matters where Parliament can legislate. The article draws the outer line of Union administration.
74: This article creates the Council of Ministers, with the Prime Minister at its head, to aid and advise the President. The President must act in accordance with that advice. The President may once require the Council to reconsider its advice. The advice after reconsideration binds the President. Courts cannot inquire into what advice the Ministers tendered. The real executive thus sits in the Council, not the formal head.
75: This article covers the appointment and responsibility of Ministers. The President appoints the Prime Minister. Other Ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister's advice. The Council of Ministers cannot exceed fifteen per cent of the membership of the House of the People. A member disqualified for defection cannot be a Minister during that disqualification. Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President. The Council is collectively responsible to the House of the People. The President administers to each Minister the oaths of office and secrecy.
76: This article creates the Attorney-General for India. The President appoints a person qualified to be a Judge of the Supreme Court. The Attorney-General advises the Government of India on legal matters referred by the President. The office also carries duties of a legal character. The Attorney-General has the right of audience in all courts in India. The office is held during the pleasure of the President.
77: This article sets how the Government of India transacts its business. All executive action is taken in the name of the President. Orders and instruments in the President's name are authenticated under rules. Properly authenticated orders cannot be questioned merely because they were not made by the President. The President makes rules for the convenient transaction of business and allocates business among Ministers. These are the Business Rules of the Government.
78: This article lists the Prime Minister's duties toward the President. The Prime Minister must communicate all decisions of the Council of Ministers on administration and on proposals for legislation. The Prime Minister must furnish information on administration that the President calls for. And any matter decided by a Minister alone must go before the Council if the President so requires. This keeps the head of State informed.
79: This article creates the Parliament of the Union. It consists of the President and two Houses known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People. The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha. The House of the People is the Lok Sabha. The President is part of Parliament though not a member of either House.
80: This article fixes the composition of the Council of States. It has not more than two hundred and thirty eight representatives of the States and the Union territories. The President also nominates twelve members with special knowledge of literature, science, art, or social service. The allocation of state seats follows the Fourth Schedule. State representatives are elected by the elected members of the state assembly by proportional representation.
81: This article fixes the composition of the House of the People. It has not more than five hundred and thirty members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States. It may also have not more than twenty members from the Union territories. Seats are allotted to the States so that the ratio of seats to population stays the same for all, so far as practicable. Population means the figures of the last published census.
82: This article provides for readjustment after each census. The allocation of seats in the House of the People and the division of States into constituencies are readjusted by law. Parliament decides the authority and the manner. By amendment, the present allocation stands frozen at the 1971 census figures until the first census after 2026 is published.
83: This article fixes the duration of the two Houses. The Council of States is not subject to dissolution. About one third of its members retire every second year. The House of the People continues for five years unless sooner dissolved. While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, Parliament may extend the term by law, a year at a time. The extension cannot run more than six months past the emergency.
84: This article sets the qualifications for membership of Parliament. A person must be a citizen of India and must make and subscribe the oath in the Third Schedule. For the Council of States the minimum age is thirty years. For the House of the People it is twenty five years. Parliament may add further qualifications by law.
85: This article covers sessions of Parliament. The President summons each House from time to time. Six months shall not pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next. This rule keeps Parliament meeting regularly. The President may prorogue the Houses and may dissolve the House of the People.
86: This article gives the President a right of direct communication with Parliament. The President may address either House or both Houses together. For that purpose the President may require the attendance of members. The President may also send messages to either House, for example on a pending Bill. The House must consider such a message with all convenient despatch.
87: This article provides for the special address. The President addresses both Houses assembled together at two moments. One is the first session after each general election to the House of the People. The other is the first session of each year. The address informs Parliament of the causes of its summons. Rules of procedure allot time for discussing it.
88: This article opens the Houses to Ministers and the Attorney-General. Each may speak and take part in the proceedings of either House. The right covers joint sittings and committees as well. A Minister who is not a member of a House does not vote there. This lets Ministers pilot business in both Houses.
89: This article provides the officers of the Council of States. The Vice-President of India is the ex officio Chairman. The Council chooses one of its members as Deputy Chairman. It does so as soon as may be after a vacancy arises. The office is refilled each time it falls vacant.
90: This article covers the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States. The Deputy Chairman vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the Council. The Deputy Chairman may resign by writing to the Chairman. Removal is by resolution of the Council. It needs fourteen days' notice and a majority of all the then members.
91: This article covers the Chairman's absence. When the office of Chairman is vacant, the Deputy Chairman performs the duties. If that office is also vacant, a member appointed by the President performs them. During the Chairman's absence at a sitting, the Deputy Chairman presides. If both are absent, the rules of procedure name a person, or the Council chooses one.
92: This article keeps the removal process fair. When a resolution for removing the Chairman is under consideration, the Chairman does not preside. The same rule applies to the Deputy Chairman. The Chairman may speak and otherwise take part in the proceedings while such a resolution is under consideration. Presiding passes to another member for that sitting.
93: This article provides the officers of the House of the People. The House chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker. It does so as soon as may be. Whenever either office falls vacant, the House chooses another member for it.
94: This article covers the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People. Each vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the House. The Speaker resigns by writing to the Deputy Speaker. The Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker. Either may be removed by a resolution of the House after fourteen days' notice, carried by a majority of all the then members.
95: This article covers the Speaker's absence. When the office of Speaker is vacant, the Deputy Speaker performs the duties. If both offices are vacant, a member appointed by the President performs them. During the Speaker's absence at a sitting, the Deputy Speaker presides. If both are absent, the rules of procedure provide, failing which the House chooses a person.
96: This article keeps the Speaker's removal process fair. While a resolution for removing the Speaker is under consideration, the Speaker does not preside. The same rule applies to the Deputy Speaker. The Speaker may speak and take part in the proceedings. In such proceedings the Speaker votes only in the case of an equality of votes.
97: This article provides salaries for the presiding officers. The Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People receive salaries and allowances. These are fixed by Parliament by law. Until Parliament makes such a law, they are paid as fixed by rules.
98: This article gives each House its own secretariat. Each House of Parliament has a separate secretarial staff. Posts common to both Houses may still be created. Parliament may by law regulate recruitment and conditions of service. Until then, the President makes rules after consulting the Speaker or the Chairman.
99: This article prescribes the oath for members. Every member of either House must make and subscribe an oath or affirmation before taking a seat. It is made before the President, or a person appointed by him for the purpose. The form is set out in the Third Schedule.
100: This article sets the voting rules of the Houses. Questions at any sitting are decided by a majority of the members present and voting. The Chairman or Speaker does not vote, except at an equality of votes. A House may act despite vacancies in its membership. The quorum is one tenth of the total members. Without a quorum, the Chair adjourns or suspends the meeting.
101: This article governs vacation of seats. No person may be a member of both Houses of Parliament. No person may be a member of Parliament and of a state legislature at once. A seat also falls vacant on disqualification, on resignation in writing to the Chair, and on absence without leave for sixty days. Periods when the House is prorogued do not count toward the sixty days.
102: This article lists the disqualifications for membership. A person is disqualified who holds an office of profit under the Government of India or a State, unless Parliament declares the office exempt. Ministers are not treated as holding offices of profit here. A person of unsound mind declared by a court, an undischarged insolvent, or a voluntary citizen of another country is disqualified. Parliament may add grounds by law. The Tenth Schedule adds disqualification for defection.
103: This article settles doubts about a member’s seat. A question whether a member has become disqualified under article 102 goes to the President. The President decides the question. Before deciding, the President must obtain the opinion of the Election Commission. The President then acts according to that opinion.
104: This article penalises unqualified sitting. A person who sits or votes as a member before taking the oath under article 99 is liable to a penalty. The same applies to a person who knows he is not qualified, or is disqualified, or is prohibited from sitting. The penalty is five hundred rupees for each day of such sitting or voting.
105: This article protects speech in Parliament. There is freedom of speech in Parliament, subject to the Constitution and the rules of procedure. No member is liable in any court for anything said or any vote given in Parliament or its committees. Publication under the authority of a House enjoys the same protection. Other powers and privileges are defined by Parliament by law. Until so defined, they remain those the House held at the commencement of the Constitution.
106: This article provides pay for members. Members of either House receive salaries and allowances. These are determined by Parliament by law. Until such a law is made, they are paid under rules made by the President. The provision keeps member pay in the hands of Parliament itself.
107: This article covers how Bills pass. A Bill may originate in either House, subject to the special rules for Money Bills. A Bill is not passed unless both Houses agree to it. A pending Bill does not lapse on prorogation. On dissolution of the House of the People, a Bill pending there lapses, and so does a Bill passed by it and pending in the Council. A Bill pending in the Council that the House of the People has not passed does not lapse.
108: This article resolves deadlocks between the Houses. A joint sitting may be called if the other House rejects a Bill. It may also be called on final disagreement over amendments, or after six months of delay. The President notifies the intention and summons both Houses together. The Bill then passes by a majority of the members present and voting. Money Bills and constitutional amendment Bills are outside this route.
109: This article gives the House of the People sole control over Money Bills. A Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Council of States. After the House of the People passes one, the Council has fourteen days. The Council returns it with recommendations. The House of the People may accept or reject them. If the Council does not return the Bill in fourteen days, it is deemed passed by both Houses.
110: This article defines a Money Bill. A Bill is a Money Bill if it deals only with taxes, borrowing, or the custody of the Consolidated Fund. It also covers charged expenditure, and the receipt and audit of accounts. Fines and licence fees do not make a Bill a Money Bill. If a question arises, the Speaker's decision is final. Every Money Bill carries the Speaker's certificate.
111: This article covers the President's assent. When both Houses pass a Bill, it is presented to the President. The President declares assent or withholds it. The President may return a Bill, other than a Money Bill, once for reconsideration. If Parliament passes it again, with or without changes, the President must assent. For a Money Bill the return option is not available.
226: This article gives every High Court wide power to issue directions, orders, or writs. The writs include habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari. A High Court can issue them for fundamental rights and also for other legal rights, which makes this power wider than Article 32. The writ can reach any person or government within the court's territories. An interim order made without notice to the other side can be vacated on application.
368: This article gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution. An amendment starts as a Bill in either House. Each House must pass it by a majority of its total membership and by two thirds of the members present and voting. The President then gives assent. Some amendments also need ratification by half the state legislatures. Courts have held that this power cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution.
21A: This article makes free and compulsory education a right for every child aged six to fourteen. The State must provide this education. A child can claim it as a matter of right, not charity. It was added in 2002 so that schooling becomes a duty of the State.
31A: This article saves certain laws from being struck down for violating fundamental rights. It covers laws about acquiring estates and similar property reforms. Land reform laws cannot be attacked merely for limiting property rights. Courts later read this saving as subject to the basic structure of the Constitution.
31B: This article protects laws placed in the Ninth Schedule from challenge under fundamental rights. Laws added to that schedule are shielded even if they conflict with Part III. In 2007 the Supreme Court held that laws added after 1973 can still be tested against the basic structure of the Constitution.
31C: This article shields laws that carry out certain directive principles. Those principles deal with sharing resources and reducing wealth gaps. Such laws cannot be struck down under Articles 14 and 19. Since 1973, the shield does not cover laws that damage the basic structure of the Constitution.
31D: This article was inserted by the Forty second Amendment to save laws against anti national activities. It never came into effect. It was omitted by the Constitution Forty third Amendment Act in 1977. The Constitution today contains no such article.
32A: This article was inserted by the Forty second Amendment and omitted by the Forty third Amendment in 1977. It had removed the power of courts to examine State laws in certain proceedings under Article 32. It never took effect and no longer exists.
39A: This article asks the State to make justice equal in practice. The legal system should promote justice on the basis of equal opportunity. The State must provide free legal aid, by law, by schemes, or in any other way. The goal is that no citizen is denied justice for want of money or other disability. The 42nd Amendment inserted this article in 1976.
43A: This article asks the State to bring workers into management. By law or other means, the State should secure the participation of workers in running undertakings or establishments engaged in any industry. The 42nd Amendment inserted this article in 1976. The idea is a voice for workers in decisions that shape their work.
43B: This article asks the State to promote cooperative societies. The State should foster their voluntary formation, autonomous working, democratic control, and professional management. The 97th Amendment inserted this article in 2012. A cooperative is a body owned and run by its members. The principle supports them without putting them under state control.
48A: This article asks the State to protect and improve the environment. It also covers forests and wildlife, which the State must safeguard for the country. The 42nd Amendment inserted this article in 1976. Courts often read it with Article 21 in cases about pollution and forests.
51A: This article lists the duties of every citizen. Respect the Constitution, the national flag, and the anthem. Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle. Protect the unity of India and its environment. Develop scientific temper and humanism. Protect public property and strive for excellence. Courts cannot punish a breach directly, but laws may be read in its light.
334A: This article controls when the women's reservation under the 106th Amendment takes effect. The reservation covers the Lok Sabha, the state assemblies, and the Delhi assembly. It comes into effect after a delimitation done for this purpose, following the relevant census figures. Reserved seats continue till the date Parliament fixes by law. Rotation follows each later delimitation. Until then, existing representation is not disturbed.
